```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

predictmeans aims to give the numbers SAS PROC MIXED gives for the same model. This page
shows which arguments correspond to which SAS options, and what has been checked.

## Options

| SAS PROC MIXED | predictmeans |
|---|---|
| `METHOD=REML` | `lmer(..., REML = TRUE)`, `lme()`, `gls()` (the defaults) |
| `LSMEANS / DIFF CL` | `predictmeans()`: `$means`, `$pairs` |
| `LSMEANS / OM` | `weights = "proportional"` |
| `LSMEANS / ADJUST=TUKEY ADJDFE=ROW`, `SIMULATE` | `adj = "tukey"`, `"mvt"` (each pair's own df; SAS's default `ADJDFE=SOURCE` uses the term's F-test df) |
| NOTE: "Estimated G matrix is not positive definite" | a message about a singular fit; `settings$singular` |
| `ESTIMATE`, `CONTRAST` | `contrastmeans()`, `pm_joint()` |
| `DDFM=CONTAIN` | `df_method = "containment"` |
| `DDFM=BETWITHIN` | `df_method = "between-within"` (`lmer`, `lme`, `gls`) |
| `DDFM=SATTERTHWAITE` | `df_method = "Satterthwaite"` (`lmer`, `lme`, `gls`) |
| `DDFM=KR` | `df_method = "Kenward-Roger"` (`lmer`, `lme`, `gls`; the default for REML `lmer`) |
| `REPEATED / TYPE=UN SUBJECT=` | `gls(..., correlation = corSymm(), weights = varIdent())` |
| `EMPIRICAL` | `vcov = "HC0"` (or `"HC3"`, `~ cluster`; `lm`/`glm`) |

`df_method = "Kenward-Roger"` (the default for REML `lmer` fits) is Kenward–Roger as SAS
computes it, with the *observed* information of the variance parameters; pbkrtest and
emmeans use the *expected* information (`df_method = "KR-expected"`). They agree in balanced
designs. With missing data they can differ: for the split plot below with one whole plot
missing, the Kenward–Roger df of a whole-plot comparison are 8.35 with `"Kenward-Roger"` (and
in SAS) and 9.25 with `"KR-expected"`. predictmeans uses the observed information because it
stays valid with missing values (Kenward and Molenberghs 1998); in simulations it kept the 5%
level where the expected information rejected 8.5% of true hypotheses.

```{r}
library(predictmeans)
Oats <- as.data.frame(nlme::Oats)
Oats$nitro <- factor(Oats$nitro)
oats_wp <- droplevels(subset(Oats, !(Block == "I" & Variety == "Golden Rain")))
fm <- lmer(yield ~ Variety * nitro + (1 | Block/Variety), data = oats_wp)
dfs <- sapply(c("containment", "between-within", "Satterthwaite", "Kenward-Roger", "KR-expected"),
              function(m) predictmeans(fm, "Variety", df_method = m, plot = FALSE,
                                       prtnum = FALSE)$pairs$df)
rownames(dfs) <- c("Golden Rain - Marvellous", "Golden Rain - Victory", "Marvellous - Victory")
round(dfs, 2)
```

The SAS values for these pairs are, in the same order: containment 9, 9, 9; between-within
9, 9, 9; Satterthwaite 8.35, 8.35, 8.10 (as here); Kenward–Roger 8.35, 8.35, 8.10.

## What was checked

The SAS program `dev/sas/pm-reference.sas` (in the package sources) fits four data sets —
Yates' oats split plot, the same with one sub-plot missing, with one whole plot missing,
and a repeated-measures trial with an unstructured covariance — with the four `DDFM`
methods: 16 PROC MIXED runs. Their output was compared with predictmeans value by value
(`dev/sas/compare-sas.R`): every variance component, LS-mean, difference (estimate, SE,
df, limits) and Type 3 F test with its df agrees with what SAS prints, to its last digit,
except LS-mean SEs that differ by about 2e-5 (relative) where the two programs stop
their REML iterations.
